issues.subcategory: fundamental sample identity contradiction
issues.description: The Methods section explicitly states participants were recruited 'through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington' with a mean age of 19.42 years (N=374), which is unambiguously a student convenience sample. Yet the Abstract, Introduction, Current Study section, Discussion, and Conclusion all characterize this as a 'national probability sample,' 'large, national probability sample,' 'general population sample,' and 'nationally representative sample.' These descriptions are mutually exclusive. This contradiction is the most critical flaw in the manuscript and invalidates the study's core comparative claim—that its results differ from prior student-sample studies precisely because it uses a general population sample.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington... the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female.

issues.subcategory: unsupported representativeness claims
issues.description: The paper repeatedly claims high generalizability based on national representativeness, but the sample is drawn from an introductory psychology participant pool. Even if this were corrected to reference the NZAVS, claiming results are 'highly generalisable' without discussing sampling weights, response rates, known demographic biases, or the restriction to New Zealand overreaches. The claim that results generalize broadly to the New Zealand population from a student sample is entirely unjustified.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.subcategory: RMSEA confidence interval excludes point estimate
issues.description: The reported RMSEA 90% confidence interval [.025, .026] is both impossibly narrow (a range of only .001) and fails to contain the point estimate of .03. A confidence interval must contain the point estimate. The interval appears to report two nearly identical values, suggesting a copy-paste or transcription error. The actual CI is missing, making it impossible to evaluate model fit precision or whether the upper bound exceeds the .05 cutoff.

issues.subcategory: poor model fit ignored
issues.description: The CFI of .86 falls below the widely accepted minimum threshold of .90 (and well below the .95 threshold for good fit per Hu & Bentler, 1999). The authors acknowledge this is 'poorer for those indices affected by model complexity' but then accept the model anyway, citing only RMSEA and SRMR. Selectively relying on fit indices that favor the model while dismissing others that indicate poor fit is not appropriate. The chi-square test is also highly significant (p < .001) with a ratio of ~16:1 (chi-square/df), all indicating inadequate fit.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.subcategory: standard error mislabeled as standard deviation
issues.description: Throughout the Results section, the uncertainty around regression/path coefficients is labeled 'SD' (standard deviation) rather than 'SE' (standard error). These are fundamentally different quantities: SD describes the spread of a distribution of scores, while SE describes uncertainty in a parameter estimate. Reporting SE as SD is a systematic terminology error that misrepresents the nature of the reported uncertainty. This appears in every parameter estimate in the results section.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01])

issues.subcategory: confidence interval inconsistent with point estimate and standard error
issues.description: For the RWA predictor, B = -.02 and SE = .01. A 95% CI computed as B ± 1.96*SE would yield approximately [-.040, -.000]. The reported CI of [-.05, -.01] is inconsistent: it is too wide, asymmetric around the point estimate, and shifted so that the estimate (-.02) is not centered. This suggests either the SE, the point estimate, or the CI bounds are incorrectly transcribed. The interval spans .04 units while 1.96*2*SE = .039, so even that roughly matches the width but the centering is wrong.

issues.subcategory: confidence interval lower bound equals point estimate
issues.description: For the lagged effect of environmentalism on RWA, B = -.01 and the 95% CI is reported as [-.01, -.003]. If the lower bound of the CI equals the point estimate, the interval is nonsensical—the point estimate must fall within the interior of the interval, not at its boundary. This indicates a transcription or computation error in the reported CI.

issues.subcategory: measure-construct mismatch across sections
issues.description: The construct label changes inconsistently across the manuscript. The abstract calls it 'willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment.' The methods section describes the measure as 'concern about environmental problems' operationalized with items about concern and perceived exaggeration of environmental problems. The results and discussion refer to 'willingness to sacrifice for the environment.' These are empirically and theoretically distinct constructs: concern/worry, behavioral willingness, and perceived seriousness are related but non-equivalent. The actual items ('How concerned are you...' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?') measure attitudinal concern and problem minimization, not behavioral willingness to sacrifice.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'

issues.subcategory: measurement non-invariance due to missing RWA item at Time 2
issues.description: One RWA item was omitted at Time 2 but present at all other time points. In a stationary cross-lagged model with time-invariant constraints, this violates the assumption of measurement equivalence across waves. The authors do not test for measurement invariance, do not explain how the missing item was handled (whether it was simply absent from the T2 scale composite, and if so, how this affects comparability), and do not acknowledge this as a limitation. This is particularly consequential because the model constrains autoregressive and cross-lagged paths to equality across time—an assumption undermined by differing scale composition at T2.
issues.quote: The item 'Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the "normal way" things are supposed to be done', was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.subcategory: listwise deletion without attrition reporting or MCAR testing
issues.description: The study spans five years with an unreported attrition structure, yet analyses use listwise deletion. Listwise deletion produces unbiased estimates only under missing completely at random (MCAR), a strong and often untenable assumption in longitudinal research. The authors provide no information about the number of participants retained at each wave, the attrition rate, demographic or attitudinal predictors of dropout, or any test of the MCAR assumption. Full information maximum likelihood (FIML) or multiple imputation would be more appropriate and is standard in longitudinal research. The deferral of all sample details to a website is insufficient for peer evaluation.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion... Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.subcategory: inappropriate causal claims from cross-lagged correlational model
issues.description: The authors conclude 'there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism' and state the findings 'strengthen our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes.' Cross-lagged panel models establish temporal precedence within a correlational framework but cannot rule out unmeasured confounds, reverse causation from unmeasured variables, or common cause explanations. The authors themselves acknowledge a potential third-variable explanation in the same Discussion section, yet the opening conclusion asserts causation. This is inconsistent and methodologically inappropriate.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism... With our findings of a temporal connection between SDO and environmentalism, this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes, and perhaps even being foundational for these attitudes.

issues.subcategory: claiming differential predictor strength without statistical support
issues.description: The authors conclude that 'SDO is a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA,' but the model comparison test they conducted to evaluate this directly yields a non-significant result (χ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126). A p-value of .126 indicates the data are consistent with equal predictive strength. The authors acknowledge the test is non-significant but then interpret the pattern of unstandardized coefficients as supporting the claim of differential strength anyway. This is circular—they rejected the formal test for significance but interpreted the same pattern descriptively as if it were confirmed.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.subcategory: contradictory significance thresholds between sections
issues.description: The Methods section states 'we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings,' but the Figure 1 caption reads 'All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.' These are contradictory—the declared threshold cannot be both .05 and .01 simultaneously. This is consequential because several results with p-values between .01 and .05 would be significant under one threshold but not the other, and the figure caption implies a stricter standard was actually applied.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings... All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.subcategory: large sample size claim inconsistent with N=374
issues.description: The authors justify adopting p < .05 as their significance threshold 'because of the large sample size of this dataset,' and the chi-square statistic (χ²(2279) = 36511.73) implies a very large N (which would be consistent with the actual NZAVS). However, the Methods section reports only 374 participants. A chi-square of 36511 on 2279 df cannot be produced by a sample of 374 under any realistic model. This inconsistency suggests the actual sample may be substantially larger than the 374 reported, further confirming that the Methods section incorrectly describes the sample.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study... χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001... Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05

issues.subcategory: duplicate sentence in methods
issues.description: The Data Analysis section contains a verbatim repeated sentence: 'We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point' and then, two sentences later, 'Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.' This duplication suggests a cut-and-paste error during writing and may obscure an intended description of a distinct analytical step.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.subcategory: contradiction between standardized and unstandardized parameter reporting
issues.description: The Data Analysis section states 'We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances.' However, the Results section reports unstandardized coefficients throughout (denoted 'B'). Standardized coefficients are conventionally denoted β or b*. This is contradictory: the paper promises standardized estimates but reports unstandardized ones. It is also unclear why the paper would present standardized estimates that 'vary across time points' in a model where time-invariance constraints are imposed, since this would make interpreting constraint equality difficult.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances... SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001

issues.subcategory: implausible chi-square difference statistic
issues.description: The chi-square difference test comparing the SDO→RWA and RWA→SDO paths is reported as χ²(1) = 15,389.13. A chi-square difference of over 15,000 on 1 degree of freedom is extraordinarily implausible in a behavioral study and strongly suggests a formatting error (e.g., a locale-specific decimal separator where comma substitutes for decimal point, yielding 15.389 instead of 15,389). The distinction matters because 15.389 is a large but credible value, while 15,389 is not. If the latter is correct, it requires explanation; if it is a formatting error, it must be corrected.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)

issues.subcategory: five semesters versus five years discrepancy
issues.description: The Methods describes 'data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).' Five academic semesters span approximately 2.5 years, not 4–5 years. If data were collected annually across 2009–2013, that constitutes five annual waves (not five semesters). The title, abstract, and text throughout the paper describe a 'five-year' study. The 'five semesters' description is inconsistent with both the date range and the paper's own characterization of the temporal scope.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).

issues.subcategory: no pre-registration; mixed confirmatory and exploratory framing
issues.description: The paper presents some analyses as hypothesis-driven (e.g., SDO stronger than RWA, stability of attitudes) but also reports several analyses that appear exploratory (e.g., bidirectional effects from environmentalism to ideology, the asymmetric SDO-RWA relationship). No pre-registration is mentioned. The paper contains hedged language ('we may find that environmentalism also predicts changes in ideology') alongside confident confirmatory framing, blurring the distinction between planned and unplanned analyses. Without pre-registration, it is unclear which tests were specified a priori and which were conducted after inspecting results, raising concerns about inflated Type I error.
issues.quote: Drawing from both theory and this past research, we may find that environmentalism also predicts changes in ideology.

issues.subcategory: cross-lagged panel model does not separate within- from between-person variance
issues.description: The traditional cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) conflates stable between-person differences with genuine within-person change, a well-documented limitation (Hamaker et al., 2015). Significant 'cross-lagged' paths in a CLPM may reflect between-person correlations rather than within-person dynamics—meaning that individuals with higher SDO at baseline also have lower environmentalism at baseline, and this stable difference drives apparent 'longitudinal' effects. The random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) separates these components and is now considered the appropriate standard for this research question. The authors do not discuss or justify their choice of the traditional CLPM.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.subcategory: autoregressive path coefficients not reported in text
issues.description: The authors describe the autoregressive (stability) paths as their first prediction and state that 'SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time,' but no numerical values for the autoregressive coefficients are reported in the text. Readers cannot evaluate the magnitude of stability, compare it to cross-lagged paths, or assess whether the stability constraints were appropriate. These values should be reported alongside the cross-lagged estimates.
issues.quote: As shown in Figure 1, across all time points, SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time, consistent with our prediction that these variables remain largely unchanged over the study period.

issues.subcategory: theoretical mismatch between SDO items and human-nature dominance explanation
issues.description: The paper argues that the SDO-environmentalism link is explained by Social Dominants' desire for human dominance over nature. However, the paper itself acknowledges that 'items in the SDO scale exclusively frame hierarchies based on intergroup relations.' If the SDO scale only captures attitudes toward human group hierarchies, invoking 'dominance over nature' as the causal mechanism is not directly supported by the measure. This is a construct-theory mismatch: the measure cannot distinguish between dominance over nature and using nature instrumentally to dominate other human groups. The paper presents both as competing explanations without resolving which the measure actually captures.
issues.quote: On the surface, SDO appears to be of interest exclusively to research on intergroup relations and, indeed, items in the SDO scale exclusively frame hierarchies based on intergroup relations... Milfont et al. [10] argue that Social Dominants' propensity for environmental exploitation exists 'because SDO promotes human hierarchical dominance over nature'

issues.subcategory: logically inverted justification for significance threshold
issues.description: The authors state they adopted p < .05 'because of the large sample size of this dataset.' This justification is logically reversed: large samples increase statistical power and make it easier to detect trivially small effects as significant, which typically motivates adopting a MORE stringent threshold (e.g., p < .01 or p < .001) or focusing on effect sizes rather than significance. Adopting the conventional p < .05 is reasonable on its own, but the stated rationale suggests a misunderstanding of the relationship between sample size and Type I/II error.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.subcategory: reliability coefficients not labeled in table and not reported across waves
issues.description: Table 1 presents values on the diagonal (.69, .70, .76) without labeling them as reliability coefficients (e.g., Cronbach's alpha or omega) in either the table or the table note. The note references only 'numbers in square brackets' for CIs without identifying diagonal values. Additionally, reliabilities are reported only for Time 1; given the missing RWA item at Time 2 and the time-invariant model assumptions, reliability at each wave is needed to evaluate measurement quality across the study period.
issues.quote: Note. SDO = social dominance orientation, RWA = right-wing authoritarianism, WILL = willingness to make sacrifices for the environment. Numbers in square brackets represent 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 iterations. ***p < .001.

issues.subcategory: environmentalism scale has only two items without justification
issues.description: The environmentalism construct is measured with only two items, which severely limits content validity, reliability estimation (standard alpha requires at least three items; with two items it reduces to a function of their correlation), and construct coverage. No justification is provided for using only two items, no reliability metric appropriate to two-item scales is reported or discussed, and the adequacy of two items to capture the multi-dimensional construct of environmentalism is not addressed.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'
